original_question: Can there be Riemannian metrics on S^3 or S^2 × S^1 with unit volume all of whose closed geodesics are long?
target_in_paper: Question 8.8.2 (Álvarez Paiva) in §8.8, "Questions related to the systole in higher dimensions."
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right geometric setting and almost the exact opening sentence of the paper's target question: it names the two manifolds S^3 and S^2 × S^1, works in the Riemannian category, normalizes to unit volume, and asks whether one can force all closed geodesics to be long.
missing_details: The paper immediately sharpens "long" to an explicit universal bound: it asks more specifically whether every such metric has a closed geodesic of length at most 1024.

The universal quantifier should be explicit: the sharper paper-faithful formulation is about every Riemannian metric g on each of the two manifolds, not just the possible existence of a counterexample.
The volume normalization should be stated as Vol(M,g) = 1, i.e. the Riemannian volume of the metric g on M.
The manifold parameter should be made explicit as M ∈ {S^3, S^2 × S^1}.
No algebraic ambient field/ring, degree, homogeneity, nilpotency, or asymptotic quantifiers are involved here; the only data to specify are the manifold M and the Riemannian metric g.
The paper does not give a proved equivalent reformulation nearby, so the refined question should stay with the explicit formulation of Question 8.8.2.
refined_question: If M is either S^3 or S^2 × S^1, and g is a Riemannian metric on M with Vol(M,g) = 1, must (M,g) admit a closed geodesic of length at most 1024?
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of the first sentence of Question 8.8.2 in §8.8. The paper itself then makes the phrase "all of whose closed geodesics are long" precise by immediately restating the problem as an explicit short-closed-geodesic bound for unit-volume metrics. The surrounding heading shows that this is being posed as a higher-dimensional systolic-type question, and §1 supplies the paper's general conventions for geodesics and length. Since the paper does not prove an equivalent reformulation nearby, the sharp stand-alone version should simply adopt the explicit second sentence of Question 8.8.2.
